result.summary: Pausanias lists the cults, altars and tombs of the small townships of Attica, such as Alimus, Prasiae, Phlya and Acharnae. He gives local traditions, including the route of the Hyperborean firstfruits to Delos, and offers his own guesses about the names of Artemis.

scenes.title: Shrines of the coastal townships
scenes.summary: Temples and altars at Alimus, Zoster, Prospalta, Anagyrus and Cephalae, with a local explanation of the name Zoster.

scenes.title: Prasiae, Cranaus and Ion
scenes.summary: The Hyperborean firstfruits pass to Delos through Prasiae, and Erysichthon, Cranaus and Ion have tombs in Attic townships.

scenes.title: Phlya, Myrrhinus and Athmonon
scenes.summary: Many altars at Phlya and cults of Artemis at Myrrhinus and Athmonon.

scenes.title: Pausanias on Artemis's titles
scenes.summary: Pausanias, finding no clear answer from guides, guesses that the titles of Artemis come from Eubœa and from the king Colaenus.

scenes.title: Cults of Acharnae
scenes.summary: The Acharnians worship Apollo, Hercules, Athene and Dionysus under many titles.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias equates the Venerable Ones with the Eumenides.
Cephalae people call the Dioscuri the Great Gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Describes the mysterious route of the Hyperborean offerings, hidden in wheat, to Delos.

analysis.text: Pausanias gathers local cults and traditions, showing religion rooted in place and his habit of guessing when guides cannot explain.
The passage shows how varied Attic local worship was, with deme cults preserving older traditions and ties to Eubœa and Delos.

language_notes.text: "Founded by haphazard" means the townships were settled without any planned scheme; Pausanias is explaining why their records are scattered and slight.
Zoster is Greek for "belt"; the local story explains the name through Leto loosening her girdle in expectation of childbirth.
Castor and Pollux, the twin Dioscuri (sons of Zeus), were widely honoured; "Great Gods" echoes the title of the mystery deities of Samothrace.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people of the far north who sent sacred offerings to Apollo at Delos, relayed from tribe to tribe.
Refers to Pausanias' earlier account in this book of Amphictyon deposing Cranaus, an early king of Athens.
"The Venerable Ones" (Semnai Theai) was a respectful title for the Furies, called Eumenides, avoiding their dreaded name.
"Interpreters and Experts" are local guides and religious experts (exegetai) who explained sacred sites to visitors.

context_notes.text: Demeter is goddess of grain; Proserpine (Greek Persephone) is her daughter, queen of the dead. They were often worshipped together.
Ion, son of Xuthus, was the legendary ancestor of the Ionians; Athenians called him their war leader against Eleusis.
Amarynthian Artemis was worshipped at Amarynthus in Euboea, which had a famous festival of the goddess.

literary_notes.text: This brief closing remark shows Pausanias as a cautious reporter, separating inherited local tradition from his own opinion, which follows.
Pausanias presents himself as an honest inquirer who admits when guides fail him and then offers only a modest conjecture.
